cause_plain: The app crashes at startup. One route is declared with status 204 (No Content), but its function has a return type like `-> dict`. FastAPI treats that return type as the response body, and a 204 response can't have a body.
cause_technical: In fastapi/routing.py APIRoute.__init__ (lines 472-477), response_model is inferred from the endpoint's return annotation when none is given. The assert at line 514 then fails because status 204 forbids a body. The user's `@app.post("/", status_code=HTTPStatus.NO_CONTENT)` in main.py:12 hits this. The inferred model should be dropped when the status code doesn't allow a body. The edit below does that. An explicit response_model is still rejected. The user can also work around it by adding `response_model=None` to the decorator or removing the return annotation.
real_cause: get_typed_annotation() turned the string annotation 'None' (from postponed annotations) into NoneType rather than None, so the route was treated as having a response body and the 204 assertion failed.

cause_plain: Building a link with a URL value named "self" crashes with a confusing TypeError. It happens because the URL builder's own "self" argument clashes with the value.
cause_technical: Flask.url_for in src/flask/app.py (line 953) declares `self` as a normal parameter. helpers.url_for forwards **values to current_app.url_for(...). A value named `self`, as in url_for('x', self=1), therefore collides with the bound instance and raises 'got multiple values for argument self'. Making `self` positional-only lets `self` pass through **values as a query or URL value.
real_cause: Flask.url_for() declared self as an ordinary parameter, so a URL value named 'self' passed via **values collided with it; the fix makes self positional-only.

cause_plain: A POST that got redirected (for example by a 301, 302 or 303) was re-sent as a GET with no body. It still claimed the old body length. The HTTP library refused to send a request that promised 5 bytes and delivered none, so the request failed.
cause_technical: In httpx/middleware.py, RedirectMiddleware.build_redirect_request (line ~91-97) copies the old request's headers through redirect_headers. When the method changes to GET, redirect_content returns b"". The copied headers still contain Content-Length (and possibly Transfer-Encoding and Content-Type). BaseRequest.prepare sees content-length already present and does not recompute it. h11 then raises LocalProtocolError('Too little data for declared Content-Length') at EndOfMessage in http11._send_request_data. The ReadTimeout in the trace is a side effect, because the background send task failed. I did not read Headers.__delitem__. The fix assumes it ignores missing keys, as the existing `del headers["Authorization"]` call implies. The fix is untested.
real_cause: RedirectMiddleware.redirect_headers() kept Content-Length/Transfer-Encoding when a redirect switched the method to GET and dropped the body, so h11 saw too little data for the declared length.

cause_plain: Defining a class with `@define` crashed at import time with a SyntaxError. This happens when the class has a `__attrs_pre_init__` that takes arguments and also has a keyword-only field with a default. attrs wrote broken code for the class's `__init__` and Python refused to compile it.
cause_technical: In `_attrs_to_init_script` (src/attr/_make.py, around lines 2204-2215), the arguments for the `self.__attrs_pre_init__(...)` call are built from the `__init__` parameter strings, and those strings include defaults. For a keyword-only field with a default, `kw_only_args` holds `y=attr_dict['y'].default`. The code then builds `f"{kw_arg}={kw_arg}"`, which gives `y=attr_dict['y'].default=y=attr_dict['y'].default`, and that is a SyntaxError. Positional fields with defaults are also passed as `x=<default>`, so the pre-init hook would see the default and not the value the caller passed. The fix is to use only the parameter names when building the pre-init call.
real_cause: _attrs_to_init_script() built the __attrs_pre_init__ call from kw_only argument strings that still included '=default', generating invalid code like a=attr_dict['a'].default=a=....

cause_plain: Black crashed while formatting a file that has a line with a multiline string. One piece of the line was never given its bracket-nesting depth, and the line-length check assumed every piece had one.
cause_technical: In src/black/brackets.py BracketTracker.mark (lines 89-97), two early returns skip `leaf.bracket_depth = self.depth` at line 113. They are COMMENT leaves and closing brackets with no matching opener at depth 0. Such a leaf can still end up in Line.leaves. is_line_short_enough in src/black/lines.py (about line 1404, reported as 1279 in the trace) then reads `leaf.bracket_depth` on that leaf and raises AttributeError. Giving those leaves a depth in mark() fixes the cause. I did not trace which of the two cases the failing input hits, so this is a best guess.
real_cause: blib2to3 Leaf declared bracket_depth only as an annotation and neither __init__ nor clone() set it, so leaves created outside the bracket tracker lacked the attribute that is_line_short_enough() reads.
